name: couril

attributes.attribute: caught travelers and made them dance to death
left a young woman with a half-fairy child
classed by MacKillop as a gnome of Brittany
compared to the goric of the same region
found most often around the ruins of Tresmalouen

sources: Henderson, George. Survivals in Belief Among the Celts. Glasgow: James MacLeose and Sons, 1911, 73.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text:
The courils were Breton fairies. They were wicked, or plainly mischievous.
They gathered around the old stone circles, most of all those at Tresmalonen.
There they danced all night. A traveler who neared them in the dark was taken and made to dance until he fell dead from exhaustion. If the lost traveler was a young woman, the fairies enjoyed her favor and left her with child, a half-fairy child. MacKillop classes the couril as a gnome of Brittany rather than a fairy proper. He compares the creature to the goric of the same region. The ruins of Tresmalouen are the spot where the couril was found most often.

okr.objective: The courils are mischievous Breton fairies of the stone circles.
key_results: The courils were Breton fairies, evil and full of tricks.
They gathered around stone circles and danced all night.
A traveler they caught danced until exhaustion killed him.
A captured young woman bore a half-fairy child.
MacKillop classes the couril as a gnome of Brittany.
The couril is compared to the goric and haunts the ruins of Tresmalouen.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore MacKillop 2008, s.v. 'Couril'
